results.title: MRI findings in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: mammillary body atrophy and thalamic signal change

output.summary: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (WKS) can cause behavioral changes and dementia in patients with chronic alcohol use. Key distinguishing features: (1) MRI shows mammillary body atrophy and thalamic T2 signal change (periaqueductal gray involvement in acute Wernicke's phase); (2) thiamine level is low or borderline; (3) behavioral profile is predominantly amnestic (Korsakoff amnesia) rather than the disinhibition and social dysfunction characteristic of bvFTD; (4) MoCA typically shows severe memory impairment with relative frontal preservation, the opposite of bvFTD profile. Clinical correlation with neuroimaging and thiamine level is required to distinguish these entities.

findings.finding: Executive function (DKEFS): Severely impaired. Trails switching: 2nd percentile. Color-word inhibition: 1st percentile. Category fluency and letter fluency both impaired.
Social cognition (Faux Pas test): 2/10 scenarios identified correctly (<2nd percentile). Reading the Mind in the Eyes: 14/36 (<2nd percentile) — severe social cognition impairment.

Episodic memory (HVLT-R): Moderate impairment. Delayed recall 3/12 (10th percentile). Recognition 8/12 (25th percentile). Memory impairment is somewhat greater than the frontal-executive profile alone would predict.
Working memory: Digit span forward 5, backward 2 — impaired.
FBI (Frontal Behavioral Inventory, informant): 38/72 — very elevated, indicating severe disinhibition, perseveration, and apathy.

output.impression: Severe executive dysfunction and social cognition impairment. Episodic memory moderately impaired. Visuospatial function relatively preserved. FBI markedly elevated per informant. Neuropsychological profile shows selective anterior-network impairment with relative posterior sparing

findings.finding: Bilateral frontal hypometabolism — severe. Orbitofrontal cortex, medial prefrontal cortex, and anterior cingulate show 28-34% FDG reduction versus cerebellar reference. This is the most prominent metabolic deficit.
Mild bilateral anterior temporal hypometabolism (12-16% reduction).
Preserved — posterior cingulate, parietal association cortex, and occipital lobes show normal FDG uptake.
Patchy mild hypometabolism in periventricular regions corresponding to areas of white matter change.

output.impression: Severe bilateral frontal hypometabolism with preserved posterior cortex — pattern consistent with frontotemporal hypometabolism. The degree of frontal metabolic reduction exceeds what is expected from the white matter changes alone

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
required_recommendations: Optimise vascular risk factors (BP, glycaemia, lipids, OSA adherence).
Do not attribute the syndrome to remote alcohol use; ensure thiamine replete if any current intake.
Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (≥3 of 6 core features within 3 years) and document functional decline.
Assess and document decision-making, financial, and driving capacity given the high risk of impulsivity and impaired judgment in FTD.
Provide caregiver education, safety planning, and referral to FTD-focused support resources.
Offer genetic counselling and discuss cascade testing options if a pathogenic variant is identified or suspected.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

accepted: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), probable, sporadic, with concurrent small-vessel cerebrovascular disease (secondary contributor)

differential.key_features: Hypertension and diabetes plus small-vessel changes on MRI may contribute, but the dominant pattern is lobar frontotemporal degeneration.
Remote alcohol use disorder (12 years sober) is too remote to explain progressive 2-year decline; thiamine reasonable but unlikely to be the cause.
Amyloid biomarker negativity expected to exclude.

differential.diagnosis: Behavioural manifestation of treated OSA (untreated component)
differential.key_features: OSA already treated; should not produce progressive degenerative imaging pattern.

key_clinical_evidence: The frontotemporal lobar pattern is the dominant finding; small-vessel disease is a comorbidity, not the primary aetiology.
Remote (12-year sober) alcohol use does not explain progressive decline beginning long after cessation.
Aggressive vascular risk modification is beneficial regardless of the primary diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Sobriety of 12 years duration cannot produce a new progressive 2-year decline; alcohol-related dementia is not the cause.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Could mislead toward alcohol-related cognitive disorder.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive personality change, disinhibition, and inappropriate behavior — 2 years

family_history: No family history of ALS or FTD

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. T is a 61-year-old retired police sergeant with a history of remote alcohol use disorder (12 years sober, active AA member), type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and treated obstructive sleep apnea who is brought to the neurology clinic by his wife. His wife has been his primary historian, as he minimizes all reported behavioral changes and insists he is 'fine.' She describes a 2-year history of progressive personality and behavioral transformation that she initially attributed to retirement stress. Approximately 2 years ago, Mr. T began to spend increasingly long periods watching the same sports content on television — up to 18 hours per day — and became enraged when interrupted. He has lost interest in grandchildren and friends, with whom he formerly had warm relationships. He has made several sexually inappropriate comments to his wife's sister and a female neighbor, which is completely out of character for a man his wife describes as having had 'strict moral values' throughout their 34-year marriage. He made two unauthorized withdrawals totaling $22,000 from their joint retirement account, the purpose of which he cannot or will not explain. He has urinated in the backyard on multiple occasions and twice inside the house in non-bathroom locations, each time appearing unconcerned about the behavior. He has developed a fixed eating routine, consuming chips and dip at the same time every day, becoming agitated when this is unavailable. His language has become more concrete — he gives one-word answers where he formerly was verbose. His remote alcohol use disorder is well-controlled (12 years sobriety, AA attendance), making active alcoholism unlikely. He is adherent with CPAP and his wife confirms improved sleep quality. His behavioral changes — disinhibition, hyperorality, stereotypy, and loss of empathy — have progressed against a background of remote alcohol use disorder in long-term remission and vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension).

neurological_exam.additional: Wife is clearly frustrated and distressed. She states her husband has been 'a completely different person' for the past 2 years. He watches football for 18 hours a day, eating chips and ignoring family. He made two large unauthorized withdrawals from their retirement savings for undisclosed purchases. He has urinated in the backyard and twice in inappropriate household locations. He has propositioned his wife's sister. The grasp reflex is prominent bilaterally — a frontal release sign. His prior alcohol use disorder is in long-term remission (12 years sober) and he is adherent with CPAP for his obstructive sleep apnea.
